extracted.intended_audience: academic physicians, surgical trainees, and early-career researchers learning to perform peer review
extracted.subtask_short: peer review of medical research manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing constructive, ethical, and methodical peer reviews of medical (especially surgical) research manuscripts, including how to evaluate study design, statistics, reporting standards, manuscript sections, and reviewer conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize several traditional peer review models (single-blind, double-blind, open) and newer/experimental models (prepublication, post-publication, independent review services, collaborative model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the advantages and disadvantages of each model (eg, single-blind allows reviewer honesty but risks bias to authors; double-blind aims to mitigate bias but often fails to fully blind; open encourages respectful feedback but may discourage frank critique). Consider journal-specific practices for how reviews are used (kept confidential, published with manuscripts, or cascaded to other journals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess study design appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the manuscript's study design (observational, interventional, qualitative, etc.) is appropriate to answer the stated question(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider strengths and weaknesses of the design (eg, case reports are not generalizable; RCTs minimize confounding). Determine if the design matches the aims and whether conclusions are supported by the design and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply and check reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure studies adhere to established reporting checklists appropriate to the study design (STROBE, CONSORT, TREND, SCARE, COREQ, SRQR, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewer should be able to identify each checklist component in the manuscript and request missing information prior to publication. Use these checklists to promote completeness and facilitate critical appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate generalizability and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how generalizable the findings are given the study population, setting, and design and whether the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention to inclusion/exclusion criteria, sampling, and sources of bias or confounding that might limit applicability of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically appraise statistical methods and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the appropriateness of descriptive and comparative statistics, tests chosen for variable types and distributions, and data presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether data distribution justifies use of mean versus median, t-tests versus nonparametric tests, correct tests for categorical variables (chi-square vs Fisher exact), appropriate use of Kaplan–Meier/log-rank for time-to-event analysis, and whether tables/figures communicate the most salient data without unnecessary duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess multivariable analyses and covariate selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When multivariable analyses are used (odds ratios, hazard ratios, relative risks), reviewers should note which covariates were included, how they were chosen, and whether relevant covariates were omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the analyses appropriately address confounding, and watch for inappropriate causal language when only associations are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request statistician review when required
rubrics_metrics.description: If analyses are complex or there are concerns about statistical approach, the reviewer should recommend formal statistical review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation can be placed in confidential comments to the editor, particularly for more advanced methods or unclear analytic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate qualitative research on its own methodological terms
rubrics_metrics.description: For qualitative studies, reviewers should evaluate rationale, context, case sampling, data collection methods, personnel performing data collection, and how results are elevated beyond description through interpretation and integration with prior research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative reporting checklists (COREQ, SRQR) to ensure sufficient methodological detail and justification for chosen approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review book chapters for relevance and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Book chapters should provide an appropriate overview or in-depth review, be written by competent authors and reviewers, and contain comprehensive literature review and logical organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether material is relevant to the stated chapter topic, whether conclusions are supported by literature/expertise, and whether tables/figures add value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm ethical approvals and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure manuscripts include statements confirming appropriate Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics approval where required and adherence to relevant ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit ethics statements and ensure study conduct is consistent with reported approvals; raise ethical concerns to the editor if suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before accepting a review: confirm expertise, availability, and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to accepting an invitation, reviewers must ensure they have subject matter expertise, can meet the deadline, and have no personal or financial conflicts of interest that would bias the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If expertise is inadequate, a conflict exists, or the deadline cannot be met, decline or recuse. Consider journal-specific COI policies and recuse when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive, respectful, and actionable feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching goal of a review is to improve manuscript quality by providing constructive feedback in a respectful manner, including actionable suggestions even if recommending rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on big-picture scientific quality and value rather than surface grammar, and clearly differentiate major (critical) revisions from minor points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize with journal scope and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should know the target journal's scope, readership, and manuscript formatting preferences before reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the manuscript fits journal audience and format (eg, structured abstract length, section expectations) and comment when it does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty, impact, and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the work addresses an important topic, adds to existing literature, paves way for future studies, or has potential to influence clinical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these first-impression judgements (originality, novelty, importance) in the review summary when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured review strategy and systematic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a consistent systematic method to approach reviews (eg, abstract → figures → main text, or top-to-bottom), and use a clear structure to present the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommended structure includes a short summary of the manuscript and its impact, followed by section-by-section critique and delineation of major versus minor points (Table 3 checklist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique manuscript sections specifically (abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, tables/figures, bibliography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide targeted appraisals for each manuscript component: abstract should summarize and fit format; introduction should set rationale and aims; methods should define exposures, populations, analyses and reference reporting guidelines; results should be organized and avoid redundant text; discussion should place results in context and include limitations; tables/figures should have clear titles/legends; bibliography should be appropriate and current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 3 checklist items (eg, 'Does it grab the reader's attention?' for abstract; 'Are the primary and secondary aims stated clearly?' for introduction; 'Are the appropriate statistical tests used?' for methods). Suggest additional references when needed but avoid self-promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure clear and logical data presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Data should be organized logically to guide readers and support authors' conclusions; use tables/figures to communicate key data without unnecessary repetition in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify data that don't require emphasis, point out unclear or misleading presentations, and suggest additional analyses that would strengthen conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: One primary outcome and appropriate outcome reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should define one primary outcome clearly, with secondary outcomes listed separately, and outcomes reported appropriately (continuous vs categorical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check analytic approaches are suited to the outcome types and distribution and that measures of statistical significance (p-values, confidence intervals) are reported where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish major (critical) vs minor revision points
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should clearly mark which comments are critical for revision/acceptance and which are minor suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major points typically affect validity or interpretation (eg, fundamental design flaws, missing ethics approval, major statistical errors); minor points are clarifications, small analyses, or stylistic suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear recommendation and confidential comment to the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a recommendation (accept, minor revision, major revision, reject) accompanied by a brief, confidential explanation to the editor that does not merely repeat comments to authors and highlights critical concerns and needs (eg, statistical review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency between comments to authors and the confidential editorial note; use the confidential section to flag ethical concerns, COIs, or suggestions about suitability for the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to ethical guidelines for reviewers (COPE principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) guidelines and ethical issues: confidentiality, conflicts of interest, timely submission, and appropriate expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recuse when ethical violations are possible (inadequate expertise, inability to meet deadline, competing interests). Raise concerns about possible misconduct or COIs to the editor via confidential comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose and avoid conflicts of interest; journals should disclose editorial COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers, editors, and editorial board members should disclose financial and nonfinancial conflicts; individual reviewers should recuse when conflicts exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals are encouraged to publicly disclose COIs; reviewers should follow journal policy and recuse or declare competing interests that could bias the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plagiarism detection and report suspected misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that many journals use software to detect plagiarism; reviewers should also flag suspected ethical issues in study design, data collection, or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report concerns directly to the handling editor via confidential comments rather than confronting authors publicly in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote diversity and transparency in peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should support diversity in editors, editorial boards, and reviewers (gender, age, race/ethnicity, career experience, sexual orientation, geography) to reduce publication bias and strengthen review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and journals should encourage transparency about review and editorial processes and diversity initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentored reviews and training for reviewer development
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal training programs and mentored peer reviews help new reviewers develop skills; mentors should obtain permission from the handling editor for mentee involvement and remain intimately involved in drafting the final review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If formal programs are unavailable, identify experienced mentors, perform mentored reviews, and request feedback to improve review quality and readiness for editorial roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus reviews on scientific quality and avoid nitpicking language/grammar unless unreadable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should prioritize appraisal of scientific quality and value rather than grammatical or stylistic details unless poor language impedes understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor language edits can be noted, but do not let copyediting distract from bigger methodological or interpretive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop reviewer reputation and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistently reliable, timely, and high-quality reviews are noticed by editors and can lead to editorial board invitations and leadership roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to provide thorough, timely, and constructive reviews; track record may influence promotion to editorial leadership.
